references.text: The parallel text in Matthew where a leper comes to Jesus, falls down, and says, "Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean." Jesus touches him and heals him.
The parallel text in Mark about the healing of the leper who kneels and asks Jesus to make him clean.
The Mosaic law concerning leprosy in Leviticus 14, where rules for diagnosis and handling of leprosy are given – the background for understanding leprosy as uncleanness.
The Mosaic law regarding the cleansing ritual for the leper after healing. Jesus refers to this ritual when he sends the healed man to the priest (the next verse).
Miriam is struck with leprosy, and Aaron asks Moses to intercede for her. This shows that leprosy was seen as a serious condition requiring God's intervention.
Naaman the Syrian was healed of leprosy by the word of the prophet Elisha. Jesus himself mentions this event in Luke 4:27 just before this passage.
Jesus mentions Naaman the Syrian and the lepers in Israel in his sermon at the synagogue in Nazareth, shortly before this incident with the leper.
Another healing of lepers in Luke, where ten lepers cry out to Jesus and ask for his mercy, and all are cleansed.
Jesus refers to the healing of lepers as a sign that he is the Messiah when answering John the Baptist's question.
Abraham fell on his face before God. The leper's act of falling on his face is a gesture of deep reverence and worship.
Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees just before this event, showing a similar pattern of people recognizing Jesus' power and falling down before him.
